content: A disability is defined as a condition or function that is significantly impaired when compared to the usual standard of an individual or their group. This term is commonly used to describe limitations in individual functioning, which may include physical impairments, sensory impairments, cognitive impairments, intellectual impairments, mental illnesses, or various forms of chronic diseases. This perspective aligns with the medical model of disability, which focuses on the individual's condition. In contrast, the human rights or social model of disability emphasizes the interaction between an individual and their environment. This model highlights the role of societal factors, such as attitudes or accessibility, in labeling, causing, or perpetuating disability. It underscores how societal structures often favor the majority, thereby marginalizing individuals with disabilities. Disabilities can be congenital, meaning present at birth, or acquired later in life. On December 13, 2006, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. This was the first human rights treaty of the 21st century, aimed at safeguarding and promoting the rights and opportunities of the approximately 650 million people worldwide living with disabilities. These rights include access to education, employment, and cultural life, the ability to own and inherit property, protection from discrimination in marriage and family life, and the assurance that they will not be subjected to medical experiments without consent. In 1976, the United Nations declared 1981 as the International Year for Disabled Persons, which was later renamed the International Year of Disabled Persons. This initiative was followed by the UN Decade of Disabled Persons (1983–1993), which included the World Programme of Action Concerning Disabled Persons. During the planning of the International Year for Disabled Persons, Frank Bowe was the sole representative with a disability from any country. Today, many nations appoint representatives who themselves have disabilities. The UN Decade of Disabled Persons concluded with an address to the General Assembly by Robert Davila, who, like Bowe, is deaf. In 1984, UNESCO officially recognized sign language as a valid medium for the education of deaf children and youth, marking a significant step forward in inclusive education.
